usage: Used when highlighting a distinct difference between two subjects in an academic or formal argument.
example_sentences: In contrast to last year, our sales figures have doubled.
In contrast to traditional methods, this new approach is much faster.
The city centre is very quiet, in contrast to the suburbs.
In contrast to his brother, he is quite reserved.
In contrast to public opinion, the data suggests otherwise.
native_notes: Use this to show a sharp difference; do not use it to simply list similarities.

uzbek: ...dan tubdan farq qiladi / ...ga qaraganda butunlay boshqacha
usage: Used to express that something is very different from what it used to be or what was expected.
example_sentences: This modern office is a far cry from the cramped space we had before.
The current political climate is a far cry from what we were promised.
The sequel is a far cry from the brilliance of the first film.
Life in London is a far cry from my quiet village upbringing.
This project is a far cry from the success I initially imagined.
native_notes: Idiomatic expression that adds stylistic variety beyond saying 'very different'.

usage: Used to emphasize that two things are equal in a specific quality.
grammar_pattern: Subject + verb + just as + adjective + as + subject
example_sentences: Cooking at home is just as enjoyable as eating out.
This task is just as important as the one we finished yesterday.
The second hotel was just as expensive as the first one.
He is just as talented as his sister when it comes to music.
The new software is just as user-friendly as the previous version.
native_notes: Use 'just as' to add emphasis to the equality of the comparison.

usage: A highly effective transition to start a comparison or focus on a specific topic.
example_sentences: When it comes to sports, he is an expert.
When it comes to learning languages, practice is key.
When it comes to finding a job, experience often matters most.
When it comes to healthy eating, there is no one-size-fits-all approach.
When it comes to choosing a travel destination, I prefer the beach.
collocations: When it comes to the crunch
When it comes to the point
native_notes: This is a staple in IELTS Speaking Part 3 for introducing comparisons or opinions.

usage: A common way to intensify comparisons in speech.
example_sentences: Public transport is a lot more convenient than driving in the city.
This laptop is a lot more powerful than my old one.
It is a lot more difficult than I expected it to be.
The food here is a lot more expensive than at the cafe.
I find that studying in the morning is a lot more effective than at night.
native_notes: Avoid using 'more' with words that already end in -er (like 'bigger'). 'A lot more' is perfect for adjectives like 'interesting' or 'convenient'.

usage: Used when measuring or judging the difference between two things.
example_sentences: Compared to last year, the sales figures have improved significantly.
These shoes are very cheap compared to the ones in the display window.
Compared to my old laptop, this one is extremely fast.
Life here is quite affordable compared to London.
The test was fairly simple compared to what we studied last term.
native_notes: While 'compared to' and 'compared with' are often interchangeable, 'compared with' is sometimes preferred for highlighting differences, while 'compared to' is used for similarities.

usage: Used to say that two things are of the same quality or standard.
grammar_pattern: To be + on a par with + noun
example_sentences: The salary offered is on a par with industry standards for this role.
Her skills are on a par with those of a senior developer.
This restaurant is on a par with the best ones in the capital.
The new model is on a par with its competitors in terms of design.
Public transport quality here is on a par with other major European cities.
collocations: be considered on a par with
native_notes: Often used in professional or analytical contexts to show equality.

usage: Used to emphasise that something is totally different from or not as good as something else.
example_sentences: The final movie was nothing like the book I read.
He is nothing like his brother; he is much more outgoing.
The service at this cafe is nothing like it used to be.
It’s nothing like the weather we had last summer.
Your version of the story is nothing like what really happened.
native_notes: Useful for giving personal opinions in IELTS Speaking Part 1 or 2 to create a natural, conversational tone.

usage: Used to introduce an alternative, often negative, aspect of a topic you have just discussed.
common_mistakes: Confusing it with 'on the other hand' in formal essays
example_sentences: Living in London is exciting; on the flip side, it is incredibly expensive.
You get more freedom working from home, but on the flip side, you might feel lonely.
The phone has a great camera, but on the flip side, the battery life is poor.
It is a stable job, though on the flip side, it offers little room for growth.
We saved time taking the train; on the flip side, it was much more expensive.
native_notes: Excellent for IELTS Speaking to sound conversational. Avoid in strictly academic writing.

usage: Used when two things are not exactly identical but share very similar characteristics.
common_mistakes: Using it for things that are completely identical
example_sentences: Both models are much the same in terms of performance.
My routine is pretty much the same every single day.
The two candidates' policies are much the same on education.
I find that most mobile phones are much the same these days.
Even after all these years, the house remains much the same.
native_notes: It sounds more natural and less robotic than saying 'they are very similar'.

usage: Used to describe how one person or thing is different from another.
example_sentences: Unlike my brother, I prefer staying indoors on weekends.
Unlike many other applicants, she had significant practical experience.
Unlike the first experiment, this one yielded very accurate results.
The new phone is quite small, unlike its predecessor.
Unlike most people, I actually enjoy waking up early.
native_notes: This is the most common way to make a quick, natural comparison between two subjects.

uzbek: anchagina farq qilmoq / butunlay boshqacha bo'lmoq
usage: An idiomatic expression meaning something is very different from what it was before or from a standard.
grammar_pattern: Subject + be + a far cry from + noun/V-ing
example_sentences: Modern digital art is a far cry from traditional painting techniques.
The hotel we stayed in was a far cry from the pictures on the website.
This new role is a far cry from my previous job in sales.
The final product was a far cry from what we had originally planned.
Today's weather is a far cry from the cold we had last week.
native_notes: This idiom adds a sophisticated touch to your description of change or discrepancy.
russian: быть совсем другим / быть совершенно другим

usage: Used to connect two contrasting clauses in a single sentence to show balance.
example_sentences: While some people prefer cities, others find peace in the countryside.
While the cost is high, the quality is definitely worth it.
The project was successful, while the budget was slightly exceeded.
While I agree with your point, I think we need more evidence.
Digital reading is popular, while traditional books still hold their charm.
native_notes: Use 'while' as a conjunction to contrast, but don't confuse it with 'during' (time).

usage: Used to point out a clear difference between two subjects at the start of a sentence.
common_mistakes: Forgetting the comma after the phrase
Putting the subject in the wrong place
example_sentences: Unlike my brother, I prefer living in the city.
Unlike the previous version, this model has a better battery.
Unlike most students, she enjoys waking up early.
Unlike summer in Tashkent, summer in London is quite mild.
Unlike traditional books, e-readers are very portable.
native_notes: Very common in both writing and speaking to quickly establish a contrast without sounding overly academic.

usage: Used when two things are largely identical or share many core similarities.
grammar_pattern: X is much the same as Y
common_mistakes: Saying 'very same as' instead of 'much the same as'
example_sentences: The new office layout is much the same as the old one.
His approach to the problem was much the same as mine.
Life here feels much the same as it did ten years ago.
The prices are much the same as last season.
Their test results were much the same as their homework scores.
collocations: be much the same as before
native_notes: Native speakers use this to soften a comparison, suggesting there might be tiny differences but they don't really matter.

usage: Used to describe similarities between two people, ideas, or things.
grammar_pattern: X and Y share a lot in common
common_mistakes: Saying 'have a lot in common' (which is correct, but mixing the two phrases)
example_sentences: My cousin and I share a lot in common, despite our age difference.
The two political parties share a lot in common when it comes to economic policy.
These two novels share a lot in common regarding their themes of isolation.
Although they are from different cultures, the students share a lot in common.
These cities share a lot in common, especially their historical architecture.
collocations: share a lot in common with
unexpectedly share a lot in common
native_notes: A very natural, conversational way to discuss similarities; 'have a lot in common' is equally frequent.

usage: Used when placing two things together to easily observe differences or similarities.
grammar_pattern: To look at/compare X and Y side by side
common_mistakes: Saying 'side to side' (this usually means moving left to right)
alternatives: when placed next to each other
example_sentences: When you look at the photos side by side, the difference is obvious.
We compared the two reports side by side to find the errors.
Standing side by side, it was clear that one building was much taller.
Try putting the two designs side by side to see which looks better.
If you view the data side by side, you can see the growth trend.
native_notes: Used physically or metaphorically when comparing data, images, or ideas.

usage: Used when comparing two things to show they are of equal status, quality, or standard.
example_sentences: The service at this hotel is on par with the best in the country.
His qualifications are on par with international standards.
The new software is on par with the leading competitor.
Her skills are on par with those of a professional.
The cost of living here is on par with London.
native_notes: Excellent for professional or academic contexts when arguing for quality or value.

usage: Used when adding a statement that provides a contrast or perspective to the previous point mentioned.
alternatives: If you look at the other side
example_sentences: The first test was difficult. By comparison, the second one was easy.
My smartphone is quite old. By comparison, yours is lightning fast.
Housing in London is expensive. By comparison, renting in Manchester is quite affordable.
He works long hours. By comparison, my schedule feels very flexible.
The initial phase was slow; by comparison, the final stage moved very quickly.
native_notes: Usually used as an introductory phrase at the start of a sentence to link it to the previous one.

usage: Used to point out a similarity between two things or actions.
grammar_pattern: Just as + subject + verb, + subject + verb
example_sentences: Just as plants need water to grow, children need love to thrive.
He works hard, just as his father did before him.
Just as the train arrived, the rain started to pour.
Life is like a journey, just as it is often compared to a book.
Just as we expected, the meeting was postponed.
native_notes: Used to create a balanced structure in speech and writing to show parity.

usage: Used when comparing two things where one has a significantly higher quality, performance, or level of enjoyment than the other.
example_sentences: Living in the city centre is much better than commuting from the suburbs every day.
Her English speaking skills are much better than they were last year.
This new laptop is much better than my old one because it is so fast.
I think reading the physical book is much better than reading on a screen.
The public transport system in Tashkent is much better than it used to be.
native_notes: 'Much' acts as an intensifier here. Avoid using 'very' with comparative adjectives (never say 'very better'). 'Way better than' is a very common informal alternative in spoken British English.

usage: Used to state that two things are identical or extremely similar in size, value, look, or character.
example_sentences: My score in the practice test was exactly the same as last week.
His attitude towards work is the same as his father's.
This smartphone has almost the same features as the more expensive model.
My opinion on this matter is the same as yours.
The price of bread here is the same as in the supermarket down the road.
native_notes: Learners often translate directly from Uzbek or Russian and say 'the same with' or 'the same like'. In natural English, always use 'the same as' when comparing two distinct objects.

usage: Used to strongly emphasise that something is much less adjective than something else. Very high-frequency in spoken IELTS to show natural range.
example_sentences: The sequel to the movie was nowhere near as good as the original.
My hometown is beautiful, but it is nowhere near as big as Tashkent.
The grammar exam was nowhere near as difficult as I had expected.
Online classes are convenient, but they are nowhere near as engaging as face-to-face lessons.
This cheap restaurant is great, but its service is nowhere near as fast as the one next door.
native_notes: 'Nowhere near as... as' is a highly natural, idiomatic way to express a large negative comparison. It sounds much warmer and more native than simply saying 'not very'.

usage: Used to state that one thing is not like another in terms of character, appearance, or qualities.
example_sentences: Studying at university is completely different from studying at high school.
The climate in the UK is very different from the weather in Uzbekistan.
His painting style is quite different from that of his teacher.
I ordered beef, but this food tastes totally different from what I expected.
Our plans for the summer are completely different from last year's.
native_notes: While Americans frequently use 'different than', British English strongly prefers 'different from' in both academic and conversational contexts. 'Different to' is also acceptable in colloquial British speech but 'different from' is safest for IELTS.
